Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

item.title: Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss
item.description:
Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss Expert comment jon.wallace 18 November 2026

The meeting offers little for US interests, risk for Ukraine – and a sobering image for Europe and other countries. 

President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and President Vladimir Putin might be tempted to accept the comparisons being drawn between their coming talks in Shenzhen on Thursday and the Yalta summit of 1945. There, US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin set out the post-war peace, carving up the world between them – though the end of the British Empire was already inevitable. 

But this week’s meeting is no Yalta. It is showmanship. Any deals to be done are small – and they are all in China’s favour, unless Trump decides to side with Russia over Ukraine. 

For the rest of the world, particularly the UK and European Union, the display is a reminder of the urgent need to shore up regional alliances, the United Nations, and the rule of international law where possible. 

The players

Trump has most to lose from going to this summit. The US would have been better off had he not gone. Perhaps he was attracted by the image of standing shoulder to shoulder with two authoritarian leaders he seems to admire – more than he does the leaders of the US’s democratic allies. Perhaps it was the possibility of taking part in a Yalta-like exercise in shaping the world. 

If that was his judgement, it is wrong. For a start, unlike the Yalta photograph of 1945 (where the three leaders were seated, concealing the fact that the ailing Roosevelt needed a wheelchair) the US president will not be placed in the centre. That role will go to Xi, as host. But that positioning will also reflect the reality. Xi is the leader of the power with the least need of concessions from the others. 

Besides matters of presentation, by attending this meeting Trump surrenders yet again what has been since 1945 the US’s strongest card: that it has been the ‘leader of the free world’, upholding the rights of democracies and acting as a beacon to all those who espouse those principles. Instead, Trump carries the banner of ‘Might Makes Right’ to the summit. 

Unlike Trump, Putin has much to gain from this meeting. Russia is no superpower. Its economy is dwindling, with 40 per cent of production diverted to his war in Ukraine. With this summit in mind, Ukraine this week bombed Putin’s prized Kerch bridge to Crimea, built in 2014 after Russia’s invasion of the peninsula. The main span lies in rubble, blocking maritime traffic and the resupply of Russian troops fighting Ukraine. 

But standing with Xi and Trump, Putin will look like one of the three main leaders of the world, not the instigator of a war which has cost Russia almost half a million military dead, according to reports – with no end in sight.

The stakes

President Trump is a supplicant at this meeting – to the point where it is dangerous for him to enter into negotiations. He wants to talk about curbing the growth or renewal of nuclear weapons arsenals, partly with a view to bringing down cost. But China has said from the beginning this is a non-starter, given that its nuclear arsenal is far behind those of the other two. 

Trump may also want to push China on critical minerals: he has accused Beijing of not making good on the deal struck a year ago in South Korea. But as then, when he threatened tariffs only to swiftly back down when Xi threatened to withhold minerals supplies, he will find he has a weak hand.

He will be similarly on the back foot if Xi presses him to ensure the continued supply of top US chips from Nvidia, whether legally exported or through intermediaries. The defenestration of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO over a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy complicates the picture. But the fact remains, despite the weight of opinion in Congress and the opposition of Trump’s top team, Trump, Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have facilitated the chip trade with China. Should Trump try to change direction, it would not be surprising if Xi threatened to turn off minerals supply once again. 

The wars in Ukraine and Iran are not likely to get useful attention from the trio. China has no incentive to get involved in Iran, a war of Trump’s making from which he is trying to extricate the US. And Beijing is quietly stirring the conflict in Ukraine, helping Russia by buying its oil and selling it engines and components used in aerial warfare. Having Europe preoccupied with the conflict suits China fine. 

The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force. It is striking that Ukraine made a point of saying that its strike on Kerch bridge was conducted without Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite communication system, which it accuses the US of turning off or switching to slower speeds to put pressure on Kyiv. 

Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help. There is bitterness among Ukrainian officials that despite the heavy rebuff to Trump in the US mid-term elections, a Democrat-dominated Congress – while talking tougher on Putin – is unlikely to send more funds Ukraine’s way.

Europe, not present at this summit, is in the crosshairs of all three leaders. Trump remains in open dispute with European leaders over their dependency on US defence and alleged cultural decline. China is unhappy about the tariffs the EU is now considering, targeting its exports. And Russia is of course probing European unity over Ukraine. 

European leaders, including the UK, need to look hard at this trio and work out their response on security and trade. They have every incentive to work out a common front: a live war is taking place on their eastern flank, as their main security guarantor becomes increasingly unpredictable. And technological competition from China threatens to annihilate their manufacturing industries. 

Other countries will look at the same photograph and similarly count their friends and new alliances. The smaller the country, the more it needs the rule of international law and respect for international institutions. 

Xi, Trump and Putin may gather believing they dominate the world. But their meeting gives others every reason to look for ways to stand together.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian cargo ship hit by drone in Baltic Sea as Finland PM says conflict ‘spilling over’
item.description:
Vessel erupts in flames after strike in Gulf of Finland; Nato vows to defend ‘every inch’ of Polish territory. What we know on day 1,733

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.

Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”

The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.

“I can guarantee ⁠that Nato will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said in Warsaw on Saturday, after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in its territory on Friday. Poland accused the Kremlin of “intentional provocation” after the incident, as it occurred near where thousands of European troops allied with Ukraine were holding training exercises.

A meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles. “In the near future, we ​will receive ​strong support from our NATO ​allies to bolster the protection of our eastern ​border,” Polish defence minister ‌Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote ​on ​X on Saturday.

In Kyiv, residents say they are unbothered by Russian attacks on the city’s bridges, as Moscow tries to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, Dan Sabbagh reports. Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population. Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.
